en: Compiled by the Śramaṇa Xuánzé of Xìmíng Monastery.

Observe that the ultimate destiny is motionless, yet its subtle awakening is profoundly still; the Brahma-wheel silently follows the principle of non-retrogression, and the boat of compassion descends empty to cast its shadow upon those to be rescued.
This is why the advancement of virtue is held so precious, and why the sound of diligent practice is so vital.
It is from this that they act.

Those who lift their emotional realms to bear the heavy burden and point toward the ground of awakening with lofty resolve—comparable in their steadfastness to one clad in armor, and as swift as one driving a team of four horses—must surely take goodness as their yoke and lead it along the path of infinity;
they must surrender their bodies as servants and drive themselves toward the limitlessness of time.
The fleeting pleasures and tranquility of the five desires are, in truth, the poisoned wine of the three miserable realms;
whereas the toil and exhaustion resulting from the fourfold cultivation are truly the manifestation of myriad virtues.

Just as shallow trickles pierce stone and tiny drops fill a vessel, and as the diligence of drilling for fire and the gradual gnawing of wood are both achieved through the continuous accumulation of the minute until they become manifest, so too do these practices lead to observable results.
The earthworm has a frail constitution yet drinks from the spring; the crab possesses a robust form yet relies on burrows. When the steed Huahai grows weary, the hackneyed horse takes the lead.
How much more so for the mind of Mahāyāna and the practice of the Pāramitās—how could one fail to remain mindful of movement and stillness in their diligent cultivation?
Therefore, one can cast a single phrase like a torch into a thousand worlds ablaze,
or rescue a single life to swim through ten thousand surging currents.
Even if one were to dwell in the stage of the "place of fulfillment" for three *kalpas*, one would ultimately strive with even greater vigor than at the initial moment of resolve.
Although tranquility is identical to emptiness within the myriad practices, it is yet as fervently cultivated as one’s former attachments.

One does not scrutinize the ends of what one desires to practice, nor does one anxiously wait for that which is to be realized; one regards the cultivation of kalpas as numerous as motes of dust as if it were a mere blink of an eye, yet remains ever thirsty for further progress;
one views the journey through worlds as numerous as grains of sand as if it were a neighbor’s door, yet remains earnestly diligent day and night.
Thus, diligence among the various perfections is like the bit and whip held by a team of charioteers;
and right effort among the factors of enlightenment is like salt and vinegar that enhance the arrayed tripods of a banquet.
The source and foundation of the True Dharma reach here; the noble deeds of the Sages are completed herein.

Thus, upon hearing the discourse on the *śarīra* (relics), one’s appreciation for the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) finds no bounds; and when recollecting the stream of verses praising Tiṣya, this sudden surge of inspiration is truly present. The practice of the three refinements is fully encompassed, and what limit can there be to the cultivation of the six intentions? As I reverently contemplate these illustrious traces, how could I find rest?
Repeatedly chanting these profound chapters, I am ever more grateful for their luminous meaning.
This text consists of a single fascicle, and its contents were not translated from a foreign version.
I hope that by trading a moment’s time for a foot-long jade disc, I may be content to die at evening having heard the Dharma in the morning.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part XIV: The Perfection of Vigor. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great saṃgha of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, by what skillful means should they abide in the perfection of diligence?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, at the moment of first generating the mind of awakening, they should form this thought:
'Whatever I possess, whether body or mind, I shall first use it to perform beneficial deeds for others, and I shall cause all their aspirations to be fulfilled.'"
For example, a servant should think:
"Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, I must always act under the authority of my master; I should not act independently or according to my own will.
If I wish to go from the house to the marketplace or elsewhere, I must first consult my master before departing."
"One shall accept food and drink only when permitted, and in all matters one shall follow the wishes of the master.

In this way, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva desires to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should, at the very first moment of generating the mind of awakening, form this thought:
"Neither my body nor my mind should be allowed to act according to their own autonomy; rather, for whatever beneficial tasks there may be for others, I shall accomplish them all."

"In this way, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas relies upon the perfection of diligence and does not depart from the perfection of diligence; they vow to perform what is to be done for the sake of sentient beings. All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should abide in the perfection of diligence in this manner."
For example, when a person mounts and drives a horse-treasure, he thinks:

"I must not cause the person riding me to have their limbs tremble, to become weary or exhausted, or to damage their ornaments; whether turning, departing, staying, moving slowly, or moving quickly shall be entirely at the person's will. I shall protect that person so that they do not give rise to various faults such as anger or resentment on account of me."

"In this way, when the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wishes to practice the perfection of diligence, they do not act according to their own inclinations, but rather act for the benefit of others in accordance with their wishes, while still protecting them so that no afflictions or evil karma arise within themselves toward those beings."

Although that person may have previously rendered no kindness to the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas regard them as objects of gratitude and perform various deeds for their benefit.

In this way, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, in order to fulfill the perfection of diligence, protects the minds of others, acts in accordance with their intentions, and brings about various forms of benefit and happiness for them.

In this way, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas embraces the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*) and brings about the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings; like their own personal task, they are never weary or indolent. This is what is meant by the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abiding in the perfection of diligence.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in order to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes and to bring great benefit to all sentient beings, constantly and diligently practices the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, with a mind that never regresses—this bodhisattva mahāsattva is abiding in the perfection of diligence."

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in order to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes and to bring great benefit to all sentient beings, constantly and diligently trains in the contemplations of internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, and their mind does not regress, then this bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence.”

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in order to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) and to bring great benefit to all sentient beings, constantly and diligently practices the contemplation of the true suchness (tathatā), the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), the dharma-nature (dharmatā), the non-falsity, the non-alterability, the equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of dharmas (dharmaniyāmatā), the stability of dharmas (dharmasthititā), the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), the realm of space (ākāśadhātu), and the inconceivable realm (acintyadhātu), with a mind that never regresses—this bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence (vīryapāramitā).”

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in order to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes and to bring great benefit to all sentient beings, constantly and diligently trains in the contemplation that ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions existence; existence conditions birth; and birth conditions aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair—without the mind ever turning back, this bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence.”

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, desiring to swiftly realize all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna) and to bring great benefit to all sentient beings, constantly and diligently cultivates the contemplation that through the cessation of ignorance, formations cease; through the cessation of formations, consciousness ceases; through the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease; through the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; through the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; through the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; through the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; through the cessation of craving, grasping ceases; through the cessation of grasping, becoming ceases; through the cessation of becoming, birth ceases; and through the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair cease—such that their minds never regress, this bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence (vīryapāramitā).”

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in order to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes and to bring great benefit to all sentient beings, constantly and diligently trains in the contemplation of the noble truth of suffering—whether as suffering, impermanence, emptiness, or non-self; in the contemplation of the noble truth of origination—whether as cause, origination, production, or condition; in the contemplation of the noble truth of cessation—whether as cessation, tranquility, excellence, or renunciation; and in the contemplation of the noble truth of the path—whether as path, correctness, practice, or deliverance—and their mind never regresses, this bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence.”

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in order to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes and to bring great benefit to all sentient beings, constantly and diligently cultivates the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments with a mind that never regresses, this bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence.”

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, desiring to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes and to bring great benefit to all sentient beings, constantly and diligently trains in the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path, with a mind that never regresses, this bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence.”

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in order to swiftly realize the knowledge of all aspects and to bring great benefit to all sentient beings, constantly and diligently trains in the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—with a mind that never regresses, this bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence.”

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in order to swiftly realize the knowledge of all aspects and to bring great benefit to all sentient beings, constantly and diligently cultivates the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities with a mind that never regresses, this bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence.”

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in order to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes and to bring great benefit to all sentient beings, constantly and diligently trains in all dharani-doors and all samādhi-doors with a mind that never regresses, this bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence.”

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in order to swiftly realize the knowledge of all aspects and to bring great benefit to all sentient beings, constantly and diligently trains in the wisdom of the stage of pure observation, the stage of the spiritual lineage, the eighth stage, the stage of possessing vision, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of completion, the stage of the solitary realizer, the stage of the bodhisattva, and the stage of the Tathāgata, with a mind that never regresses—this bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence.”

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in order to swiftly realize the knowledge of all aspects and to bring great benefit to all sentient beings, constantly and diligently trains in the stage of practice through conviction, the stage of extreme joy, the stage of freedom from stain, the stage of radiant light, the stage of blazing wisdom, the stage of difficult to conquer, the stage of presence, the stage of far-reaching, the stage of immovability, the stage of excellent wisdom, the stage of the cloud of dharma, or the stage of equal enlightenment, with a mind that never regresses—this bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence.”

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in order to swiftly realize the knowledge of all aspects and to bring great benefit to all sentient beings, constantly and diligently cultivates the five pure eyes and the six supreme supernormal powers with a mind that never regresses, this bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence.”

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in order to swiftly realize the knowledge of all aspects and to bring great benefit to all sentient beings, constantly and diligently cultivates the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and other boundless Buddha-dharmas, with a mind that never regresses—this bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence.”
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in order to make the buddha-field supremely pure and adorned, dwells for a long time in saṃsāra cultivating all manner of meritorious virtues with a mind free from regression, this bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence (vīryapāramitā)."

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of bringing many classes of sentient beings to maturity, dwells for a long time in saṃsāra cultivating various merits with a mind free from retrogression, this bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence.”

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva has first resolved upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to become bodhisattvas—whether bound to one more birth, two more births, three more births, or four more births before attaining buddhahood—and they were to say:
'You should diligently cultivate the bodhisattva practices; you must first realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and only then shall I realize unexcelled awakening.'"

At that time, the bodhisattva, in accordance with those words, applies himself with diligence and valor, his mind free from fear; this bodhisattva mahāsattva thus abides in the perfection of diligence.

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is bound to only one more birth, or two more births, or three more births, or four more births before attaining buddhahood, and suppose all the sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to first resolve upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening and say:
‘You must wait until I have first realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete bodhi; only then should you realize unsurpassed awakening.’”

At that time, the bodhisattva, in accordance with those words, dwells for a long time within saṃsāra without his mind ever becoming discouraged; this bodhisattva mahāsattva thus abides in the perfection of diligence.
"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees a beggar come seeking something, their face does not knit in frown and their eyes show no sign of anger, but instead think:
'This sentient being accords with my pursuit of the knowledge of all modes; I shall quickly employ skillful means and diligently seek to give it to them.'"
This bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of diligence.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to even a single sentient being, should undergo various intense sufferings within the great hells for an eon or more than an eon, yet their body remains unmoving and their mind does not falter or retreat, this bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of diligence.

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to have days and nights equal in duration to a great kalpa, and were to accumulate such days and nights until they again formed a great kalpa, and were to remain in the great hells undergoing various intense sufferings for as long as the time span of that many Ganges-sand-like great kalpas—should he do so for the sake of enabling even a single sentient being to escape the hells and be born in a happy realm, the bodhisattva would joyfully undergo those sufferings; this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of diligence.”

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this teaching, leaps for joy and exults, vowing to receive it with a mind free from retreat or dejection, one should know that he is called a bodhisattva of diligence who abides in the perfection of diligence."

"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, upon hearing such matters, feels timid and weak in mind, failing to give rise to joy or the resolve to practice and undertake them, should be known as a 'lazy' bodhisattva."

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing of various virtuous deeds, maintains a continuous succession of thoughts that delight in and practice them, it should be known that this is called a bodhisattva of diligence abiding in the perfection of diligence."

"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, upon hearing of various wholesome deeds, is unable to maintain continuous mindfulness and practice them accordingly, one should know that such a person is called a lazy bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Suppose a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to sweep this land of Jambudvīpa from one place to another until it has been swept all around, and then return to the original spot, thinking:
'I have been away from here for a long time. "
One should know that such a person is called a "lazy bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, having set out for this purpose, should think:
"I shall return here as quickly as possible," [he is likewise so designated].
"One should know that such a person is called a bodhisattva of diligence who dwells securely in the perfection of diligence.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having spent a single day constructing or repairing a stūpa, should think:
'Why is this day so exceedingly long?'"
One should know that such a person is called a "lazy bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, having engaged in these matters, should think:
"How can this day be as brief as the snap of a finger?"
One should know that this is called a bodhisattva of diligence who dwells securely in the perfection of diligence.
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having spent a single day constructing or repairing a monastery, should think:
'Why is this day so exceedingly long?'"
One should know that such a person is called a lazy bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, having engaged in these matters, should think:
"How can this day be as brief as the snap of a finger?"
"One should know that such a person is called a bodhisattva of diligence who abides in the perfection of diligence.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, having practiced for half a year, perceives their undertaken activities as something long-standing, one should know that such a person is called a bodhisattva of indolence."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives the work performed over half a year as being the same as the work performed in a single day, one should know that this is called a bodhisattva of diligence who abides in the perfection of diligence (vīryapāramitā).
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when reflecting on the activities performed over the course of a year, develops the notion of long duration, one should know that this is called a 'lazy' bodhisattva.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when reflecting on the activities performed over the course of a year, regards them as being like activities performed in a single day, one should know that this is called a 'diligent' bodhisattva who dwells in the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā)."
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when observing the activities performed over half an eon, conceives the notion that they are long-lasting, he should be known as a lazy bodhisattva.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when observing the activities performed over half an eon, regards them as being like the activities performed in a single day, he should be known as a diligent bodhisattva who abides in the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā).”
"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, when contemplating the activities performed over the course of an eon, develops a perception of long duration, one should know that this is called a 'lazy' bodhisattva.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, when contemplating the activities performed over the course of an eon, regards them as being like activities performed in a single day, one should know that this is called a 'diligent' bodhisattva who dwells in the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā)."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate the practices for awakening, they should not contemplate the number of kalpas, thinking: 'I shall realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening after passing through such a number of kalpas.'"

"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva conceives of the number of eons as a limited duration, yet exerts themselves with diligence and vigor to cultivate the practices for awakening and seeks to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should be known as a 'lazy' bodhisattva."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

"Even if it takes immeasurable and boundless great kalpas of courageous and vigorous practice of the bodhi-path before I realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, I must certainly not allow my mind to become discouraged; I shall diligently seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."

It should be known that such a one is called a Bodhisattva of diligence who dwells in the perfection of diligence (*vīryapāramitā*), practices the perfection of diligence, swiftly brings it to fulfillment, distances himself from birth and death, is able to quickly realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), and brings great benefit to all sentient beings.

"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva conceives of the number of eons as a finite limit, then even though they are extremely courageous and constantly and diligently practice the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, they are nonetheless called a 'lazy' bodhisattva."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

"Even if it takes immeasurable and boundless great kalpas, and only after most supremely courageous and constant diligent cultivation of the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom do they become complete and one realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I must certainly not allow my mind to give way to despondency."
"You should know that such a person is called a bodhisattva of diligence who dwells securely in the perfection of diligence, and is able to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, however, establishes a limit by calculating the number of eons, then even if they are extremely courageous and constantly and diligently train in the wisdom of internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, they are nevertheless called a lazy bodhisattva."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

"Even if it takes immeasurable and boundless great kalpas, and only after attaining the perfection of the wisdom of inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence through the utmost valor and constant diligent cultivation, shall I realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I must certainly not allow my mind to give way to despondency."
"You should know that such a person is called a bodhisattva of diligence who dwells securely in the perfection of diligence, and is able to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, however, establishes a limit by calculating the number of kalpas—even if they are extremely courageous and constantly and diligently train in the wisdom of the true suchness (tathatā), the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), the dharma-nature (dharmatā), the non-falsity, the non-alteration, the equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm—they are nevertheless called a bodhisattva of indolence."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

"Even if it takes immeasurable and boundless great kalpas, and through the utmost valor and constant diligent cultivation, one must attain the perfection of wisdom regarding the suchness of all phenomena up to the inconceivable realm before realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I must certainly not allow my mind to become discouraged."

"You should know that such a person is called a bodhisattva of diligence who dwells securely in the perfection of diligence, and is able to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes of being (*sarvajñajñāna*).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, however, establishes a limit by calculating the number of eons, even if they are extremely courageous and constantly and diligently train in the wisdom that [understands] ignorance conditions formative forces (*saṃskāra*), formative forces condition consciousness (*vijñāna*), consciousness conditions name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), name-and-form conditions the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), the six sense bases condition contact (*sparśa*), contact conditions feeling (*vedanā*), feeling conditions craving (*tṛṣṇā*), craving conditions grasping (*upādāna*), grasping conditions becoming (*bhava*), becoming conditions birth (*jāti*), and birth conditions old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)—they are nevertheless called a bodhisattva of indolence."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

"Even if it takes immeasurable and boundless great kalpas, and through the utmost valor and constant diligent cultivation, the wisdom regarding the conditions from ignorance leading to formations up to birth leading to aging and death must first be perfected before one realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I must certainly not allow my mind to become discouraged."

"You should know that such a person is called a Bodhisattva of diligence who dwells securely in the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), and is able to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).

If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, however, establishes a limit by calculating the number of eons, then even if they are extremely courageous and constantly and diligently train in the wisdom that realizes the cessation of ignorance leads to the cessation of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); the cessation of volitional formations leads to the cessation of consciousness (*vijñāna*); the cessation of consciousness leads to the cessation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); the cessation of name-and-form leads to the cessation of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); the cessation of the six sense bases leads to the cessation of contact (*sparśa*); the cessation of contact leads to the cessation of feeling (*vedanā*); the cessation of feeling leads to the cessation of craving (*tṛṣṇā*); the cessation of craving leads to the cessation of grasping (*upādāna*); the cessation of grasping leads to the cessation of becoming (*bhava*); the cessation of becoming leads to the cessation of birth (*jāti*); and the cessation of birth leads to the cessation of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)—such a person is nevertheless called a Bodhisattva of indolence."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

"Even if it takes immeasurable and boundless great kalpas, and through the utmost valor and constant diligent cultivation, one must attain the perfection of the wisdom that 'because ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease,' up to 'because birth ceases, aging and death cease,' before realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I must certainly not allow my mind to give way to despondency."

"You should know that such a person is called a bodhisattva of diligence who dwells securely in the perfection of diligence, and is able to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, however, establishes a limit by calculating the number of eons, then even if they are extremely courageous and constantly and diligently cultivate the wisdom of the Noble Truth of Suffering—whether as suffering, impermanence, emptiness, or non-self—the wisdom of the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering—whether as cause, accumulation, production, or condition—and the wisdom of the Noble Truth of Cessation—whether as cessation, tranquility, excellence, or renunciation—and the wisdom of the Noble Truth of the Path—whether as path, correctness, practice, or the way out—they are nevertheless called a lazy bodhisattva."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

"Even if it takes immeasurable and boundless great kalpas, through the utmost valor and constant diligent cultivation of the knowledge of the Noble Truth of Suffering—whether as suffering, impermanence, emptiness, or non-self—and so on up to the knowledge of the Noble Truth of the Path—whether as the path, suchness, practice, or the way of emergence—until this is perfected and I realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I must certainly not allow my mind to become discouraged."

"You should know that such a person is called a bodhisattva of diligence who dwells securely in the perfection of diligence, and will swiftly be able to realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, however, establishes a limit by calculating the number of eons, then even if they are extremely courageous and constantly and diligently practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, they are still called a bodhisattva of indolence."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

"Even if it takes immeasurable and boundless great eons, and through the utmost valor and constant diligent cultivation of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments until they are perfected, before I can realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I must certainly not allow my mind to become discouraged."
"You should know that such a person is called a bodhisattva of diligence who dwells securely in the perfection of diligence, and is able to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, however, establishes a limit by calculating the number of kalpas, then even if they are extremely courageous and constantly and diligently train in the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path, they are nevertheless called a bodhisattva of indolence."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

"Even if it takes immeasurable and boundless great kalpas, and even if I must attain perfection only after practicing with supreme vigor and constant diligence the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, and only then realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I must certainly not allow my mind to become discouraged."
"You should know that such a one is called a bodhisattva of diligence who dwells securely in the perfection of diligence, and is swiftly able to realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva establishes a limit by calculating the number of eons, then even if they are extremely courageous and constantly and diligently train in the three doors of liberation, they are nevertheless called a bodhisattva of indolence."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

"Even if it takes immeasurable and boundless great kalpas, and only after most supremely courageous and constant diligent cultivation of the three gates of liberation reaches fulfillment, shall I realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I must certainly not allow my mind to give way to despondency."

"You should know that such a person is called a bodhisattva of diligence who abides in the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā) and is able to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, however, establishes a limit by calculating the number of kalpas, then even if they are extremely courageous and constantly and diligently cultivate the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa), the eight bases of mastery (aṣṭābhibhvāyatana), the nine successive attainments (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti), and the ten totalities (daśakṛtsnāyatana), they are nonetheless called a bodhisattva of indolence."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

"Even if it takes immeasurable and boundless great kalpas, and even if one must attain perfection only after practicing with the utmost courage and constant diligence the eight liberations up to the ten totalities before realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I must certainly not allow my mind to become discouraged."
"You should know that such a one is called a Bodhisattva who abides in the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā) and is swiftly able to realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva conceives of the number of eons as a finite limit, then even if they are extremely courageous and constantly and diligently train in the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi, they are nevertheless called a Bodhisattva who is indolent."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

"Even if it takes immeasurable and boundless great kalpas, and through the utmost valor and constant diligent cultivation of the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi, I must attain fulfillment before realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I must certainly not allow my mind to give way to despondency."

"You should know that such a person is called a bodhisattva of diligence who dwells securely in the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), and is able to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, however, establishes a limit by calculating the number of eons, then even if they are extremely courageous and constantly and diligently train in the various bodhisattva stages (*bhūmi*) and the wisdom of those stages, they are still called a bodhisattva of indolence."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

"Even if it takes immeasurable and boundless great kalpas, and through the utmost heroism and constant diligent cultivation of the various bodhisattva stages and the wisdom of those stages, one must attain perfection before realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I must certainly not allow my mind to become discouraged."
"You should know that such a person is called a bodhisattva of diligence who dwells securely in the perfection of diligence, and is able to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, however, establishes a limit by calculating the number of kalpas—even if they are extremely courageous and constantly and diligently cultivate the five pure eyes and the six supreme supernatural powers—they are nonetheless called a bodhisattva of indolence."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

"Even if it takes immeasurable and boundless great kalpas of most extreme diligence and constant, earnest cultivation to perfect the five pure eyes and the six supreme supernormal powers before realizing unsurpassed, right, and complete enlightenment, I must certainly not allow my mind to become discouraged."
"You should know that this is called a Bodhisattva of diligence who dwells securely in the perfection of diligence, and who is swiftly able to realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, however, establishes a limit by calculating the number of kalpas—even if they are extremely courageous and constantly and diligently cultivate the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, and four analytical knowledges—they are still called a Bodhisattva of indolence."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

"Even if it takes immeasurable and boundless great kalpas, through the utmost heroism and constant diligent cultivation of the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, and four analytical knowledges until they are perfected, before I can realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I must certainly not allow my mind to succumb to despondency."

"You should know that such a person is called a bodhisattva of diligence who dwells securely in the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), and is able to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, however, establishes a limit by calculating the number of kalpas, then even if they are extremely valiant and constantly and diligently cultivate great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity, as well as the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, they are nevertheless called a lazy bodhisattva."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

"Even if it takes immeasurable and boundless great kalpas, and through the utmost valor and constant diligent cultivation of great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity, as well as the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, before they are perfected and one realizes unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I must certainly not allow my mind to give way to despondency."
"You should know that this is called a bodhisattva of diligence who dwells securely in the perfection of diligence, and who is swiftly able to realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva establishes a limit by calculating the number of eons, then even if they are extremely courageous and constantly and diligently train in the quality of non-forgetfulness and abide in equanimity, they are still called a bodhisattva of indolence."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

"Even if it takes immeasurable and boundless great kalpas, and only after practicing with the utmost courage and constant diligence until the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of ever-abiding equanimity are perfected, shall I realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—I must certainly not allow my mind to give way to despondency."
"You should know that such a person is called a bodhisattva of diligence who abides in the perfection of diligence, and is able to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva establishes a limit by calculating the number of kalpas, even if they are extremely courageous and constantly and diligently train in the knowledge of all modes, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects, they are nonetheless called a bodhisattva of indolence."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

"Even if it takes immeasurable and boundless great eons, and even if one must attain fulfillment only after constantly and diligently training in all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) with the utmost valor, before finally realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I must certainly not allow my mind to become discouraged."

"You should know that such a person is called a bodhisattva of diligence who dwells securely in the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā) and is swiftly able to realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva establishes a limit by calculating the number of kalpas, even if they are extremely courageous and constantly and diligently practice all the conducts of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, they are nevertheless called a bodhisattva of indolence."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

"Even if it takes immeasurable and boundless great kalpas, and even if one must attain fulfillment only after constantly and diligently practicing all the bodhisattva mahāsattva deeds with supreme valor, before finally realizing unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I should not allow my mind to give way to despondency."
"You should know that this is called a bodhisattva of diligence who dwells securely in the perfection of diligence and is swiftly able to realize the knowledge of all modes.
Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!"
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is exhorted with these words:
"You should, for my sake, split apart Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains,
in a single day," and if one were to ask in return:
"O King of Mountains, how large are you?
How many parts shall I divide you into?
One who acts thus should be known as a "lazy bodhisattva."
If you should think:
"I can, in a single day, split apart Sumeru, the King of Mountains, according to its size—whether large or small—until it is the measure of a mustard seed or like an atom."
"Although it takes a vast amount of time to finally break them apart, he perceives it as being like the snap of a finger; such a one should be known as a Bodhisattva of diligence.
If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva reflects thus:

'Suppose a number of great kalpas equal to the sands of the Ganges were made into a single day and night, and by accumulating these days and nights, another great kalpa were formed; even if one were to practice the Bodhisattva path for such immeasurable great kalpas, only then would one realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.'"
"Even in this matter my mind does not waver; how much less would I fail to strive diligently when such a thing exists!
One should know that such a person is called a Bodhisattva of Diligence.

"If, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva hears such descriptions of the characteristics of diligence, they are filled with joy and exultation, their heart being free from fear or dread, one should know that they are called a Bodhisattva of Diligence."

If, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva hears such an exposition of the characteristics of diligence, their mind retreats and sinks, giving rise to deep terror, it should be known that they are called a lazy bodhisattva and will not swiftly attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing the teaching on the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā), reflects thus:
'When shall I accomplish such extraordinary and difficult-to-realize merit?'"
One should know that such a person is called a "lazy bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing the teaching of the perfection of diligence (vīryapāramitā), reflects thus:
"I possess all such merits; I must certainly cultivate them so as to reach the further shore."
"One should know that such a person is called a Bodhisattva of Diligence.
If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is approached by someone who begs for their hand, or foot, or head, they should think:
'If I give these to them, I shall be without hands, without feet, and without a head.'"
One should know that such a person is called a lazy bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has someone come to beg for their hand, or foot, or head, they should think:
"By giving these to them, I shall obtain the unsurpassed, subtle, and wondrous hands, feet, and head of devas, humans, asuras, and others."
One should know that such a person is called a Bodhisattva of Diligence.
"If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is asked for his eyes or ears, he thinks to himself:
'If I give these to him, I shall be left without eyes or ears.'"
One should know that such a person is called a "lazy bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, when someone comes to beg for their eyes or ears, thinks:
"By giving these to them, I shall attain the unsurpassed eyes and ears of devas, humans, asuras, and others, which are like supreme wisdom."
"You should know that such a person is called a Bodhisattva of Diligence, who stays far removed from the Two Vehicles and draws near to All-Knowledge (sarvajñatā).
If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is asked for various parts of his body or limbs, he should think:
'If I give these to him, I will be deprived of my various bodily parts and limbs.'"
One should know that such a person is called a "lazy bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is asked for various parts of his body or limbs, he should think:
"If I bestow these upon him, I shall obtain the branches and limbs of the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma, the dharma-body of omniscience, belonging to the devas, humans, asuras, and others."
One should know that such a person is called a bodhisattva of diligence.
"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva encounters various supplicants coming to beg for this or that, he then forms this thought:
'The supplicants are so numerous; how can I cause the wishes and intentions of all to be fulfilled?'"
One should know that such a person is called a "lazy bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, when various supplicants come seeking this or that, thinks: "This is not much;

even if all the sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were to come to me at once on a single day seeking various things, I would employ skillful means to seek out precious wealth and give it to them all, satisfying them completely—how much more so now for such a small amount! [that one should not fail to give.]
"You should know that such a person is called a Bodhisattva of Diligence. Why is this?

Because while Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas desire to manifest immeasurable Buddha-dharmas and the dharmas of omniscience, these immeasurable Buddha-dharmas and dharmas of omniscience cannot be manifested through limited diligence and giving. One must don the vast armor of immeasurable diligence and giving; only then can one manifest immeasurable Buddha-dharmas and the dharmas of omniscience."

For example, suppose there is a person who wishes to cross the great ocean; they must first prepare various provisions extending for many yojanas, many hundreds of yojanas, many thousands of yojanas, and many hundreds of thousands of yojanas, and only then will they be able to cross it.

In this way, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment must, after accumulating the provisions for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, only then realize it.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva thinks to themselves:
"I shall seek to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment throughout a great kalpa that is finite and limited," one should know that such a person is called a lazy bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:
"I shall seek to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment throughout immeasurable and boundless great kalpas," one should know that such a person is called a bodhisattva of diligence.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is such diligence on the part of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to be considered difficult?”
The World-Honored One said:
"Do you consider such diligence on the part of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to be not difficult?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied:
“I consider such diligence by the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to be no difficulty. Why is this?

The Buddha has taught that all phenomena are like illusory things; since pleasant feelings, painful feelings, and the factors conducive to feeling are all like illusions, what difficulty could there be in diligence for a bodhisattva who has already realized the true nature of all such phenomena?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:

“You should know that although the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas knows that all phenomena are like illusory things, they are nonetheless able to initiate physical and mental diligence and abide in the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*). In seeking great enlightenment, they never falter or grow weary; for this reason, such diligence by the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is most exceedingly difficult.”
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary!
World-Honored One!"
"How marvelous!
Well-gone One!
You have excellently explained how the diligence of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is exceedingly difficult."

It should be known that the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas performs what is difficult to do: although they know that all phenomena are utterly non-existent, they seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, desiring to expound for the sake of infinite sentient beings the true Dharma that can forever sever ignorance.

However, that which is called "ignorance" does not truly exist; nor is there any real dharma that could cause ignorance to grasp at a self or what belongs to a self. Furthermore, there is no sentient being who can think:
"This is my true self and what belongs to me."

"In this way, because of the convergence of conditions, there is arising, yet in reality there is no arising; because of the separation of conditions, there is cessation, yet in reality there is no cessation.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, despite knowing this, has no regression in mind, this bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā) and should be known as a 'diligent bodhisattva'."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:
"All phenomena are empty; why should I now exert myself in the perfection of diligence?"
One should know that such a person is called a lazy bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:

"Because all phenomena are ultimately empty, I seek unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; having realized the emptiness of all phenomena, I shall teach it to sentient beings so that they may be liberated from the manifold sufferings of birth and death within the five destinies."
One should know that such a person is called a Bodhisattva of Diligence.
"If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva forms this thought:
'Birth and death are without end; how could I possibly cause all beings to attain parinirvāṇa?'"
One should know that such a person is called a "lazy bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should think:
"Birth and death have no beginning but may have an end; I might as well not bring all beings to extinction."

Even if one were to seek great enlightenment through diligent effort for as many eons as have passed since beginningless time before finally attaining it, I would still seek it; how much more so if it does not require such a number of eons!
Furthermore, he formed this thought:

"If bodhisattvas delight in cultivating the mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), they will pass through days and nights, half-months, months, seasons, years, and pairs of years without perceiving or knowing it, even for as long as it takes to resolve upon the mind of enlightenment.

If bodhisattvas delight in cultivating the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, purifying their minds without forming any such mental engagement, they will likewise pass through days and nights, half-months, months, seasons, years, and pairs of years without realizing it. Therefore, since awakening is very easy to attain, one should not fear that the duration of diligent practice will be long."
"You should know that such a person is called a Bodhisattva of Diligence.
For example, it is like an elder who seeks great wealth and treasures; day and night he applies himself with diligence, contemplating skillful means, and constantly thinks:
'When shall I obtain much wealth and treasure so as to fulfill my original vow?'"
"Because of this, there is no leisure to seek food or drink.

Thus, the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, wishing to bring about the purification of the mind regarding the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) and diligently practicing the mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), passes days, nights, half-months, months, seasons, years, and pairs [of seasons] in the mere duration of a single thought-moment. They constantly reflect:
'When shall I obtain the jewel of omniscience to benefit sentient beings?'"
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

“That the assembly of bodhisattvas is able to don such great armor of diligence, seeking the jewel of the unsurpassed qualities of a Buddha to benefit sentient beings—this is truly as the World-Honored One has always proclaimed: all bodhisattvas are capable of performing what is difficult.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, saying:

“I observe the multitudes of gods, humans, and others in the world, and there are none who have accomplished such rare merit as these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, with the sole exception of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra rose from his seat, bared his left shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words:

"May all sentient beings dwelling in the boundless worlds of the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, above, and below, who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle, who have not yet resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, swiftly resolve their minds upon it;
and may those who have already resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta never again fall back."
"If those who have already become non-retrogressive regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may they swiftly fulfill the knowledge of all modes.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, saying:
"Based on what meaning do you wish that all bodhisattvas should swiftly fulfill the knowledge of all modes?"
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
“If there were no bodhisattvas, then no Buddhas would appear in the world; if no Buddhas appeared in the world, then there would be no bodhisattvas nor the assembly of śrāvakas.”
It is because there are bodhisattvas who practice the bodhisattva path that the Buddhas appear in the world;
and because the Buddhas appear in the world, there are bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas.

For example, just as a great tree possesses branches and leaves because it has roots and a trunk, and possesses flowers and fruit because it has branches and leaves, and from those flowers and fruit, a great tree is born once again.
Thus, because there are bodhisattvas in the world, buddhas appear in the world;
because buddhas appear in the world, there are bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas;
and because bodhisattvas cultivate the bodhisattva practices, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas further appear in the world to bring about great benefit.
At that time, the Buddha praised Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"It is as you have said.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should receive and uphold the perfection of diligence practiced by the assembly of bodhisattvas who have donned the armor of diligence; do not let it be forgotten or lost!"
Ānanda said: “So be it, World-Honored One!”
"I have already received and upheld the perfection of vigor practiced by the assembly of bodhisattvas who have donned the armor of diligence; I shall certainly never forget it!

When the Bhagavān had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Ānanda, as well as the other śrāvakas, the assembly of bodhisattvas, and all others—the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and so forth—having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced, and they faithfully accepted and practiced it.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Five Hundred and Ninety.
